analysis.title: "Wealth Effects" Are Overhyped
key_insights: Dario Perkins argues equity wealth effects on US consumption are weak and no longer visible in the data. The Fed's forecasting model implies a 30% rise in US stocks adds roughly 50bps to GDP, and TS Lombard disputes this.

The historical inverse link between wealth and the saving rate disappeared after the GFC. TS Lombard's own consumption function shows the coefficient on wealth collapsed over time and is no longer statistically significant.
TS Lombard attributes the breakdown to post-GFC wealth gains coming from stocks rather than housing. Equity wealth is concentrated among top income groups with low marginal propensities to consume.

The Fed's model is estimated over a long horizon with parameters flattered by the 2000s, when home equity extraction pushed the saving rate negative. Jason Furman acknowledged a residual now exists in the Fed's equation.
If wealth effects are weak, the AI-driven boost to US GDP is smaller than commonly believed, and a stock market bust would hurt consumption less than the Fed's model implies.
Greenspan promoted wealth effects during the dotcom era, but consumption kept rising after the dotcom bust, which TS Lombard cites as evidence the effect is not real.

Wealth effects are only one channel from equities to the economy. A sequel to the Perkini Report, due later this week, will examine risks around TS Lombard's crash scenario and address client feedback that it was both too bearish and not bearish enough.

macro_indicators.indicator: GDP impact of a 30% rise in US stocks (Fed model)
macro_indicators.interpretation: The Fed model's wealth effect estimate, which TS Lombard argues overstates the equity-to-consumption link and so overstates the AI-driven GDP boost.

macro_indicators.indicator: AI contribution to US GDP (Furman admission)
macro_indicators.interpretation: Furman conceded the figure after the import adjustment TS Lombard had argued for. The report gives no unit or period, so it is cited as written.

risk_factors: A stock market crash can still affect the economy through channels other than wealth effects, which the upcoming Perkini Report sequel will examine.
The Fed's model carries a residual, so its estimates of equity-driven GDP and consumption effects may be unreliable.
cross_bank_references: Jason Furman and the Fed's forecasting model hold that wealth effects are material, a view TS Lombard disputes.

key_data_points.source_bank: Federal Reserve model, as cited by TS Lombard
key_data_points.context: Model-based estimate that TS Lombard argues is not visible in the data.
key_data_points.anchor: when you model e.g. a 30% rise in US stocks, that adds roughly 50bps to GDP.

key_data_points.metric: AI contribution to US GDP acknowledged by Jason Furman
key_data_points.context: Furman acknowledged the figure last week after the import adjustment. Unit and period are not given in the report.
key_data_points.anchor: as JF finally acknowledged last week. (0.3? Really?)

tension_points.bull_case: The Fed's model, based on data since the 1960s, and Furman hold that rising stock prices make people feel wealthier and save less, which adds about 50bps to GDP for a 30% equity rise.
tension_points.bear_case: TS Lombard finds the wealth-savings link disappeared after the GFC and the wealth coefficient is no longer significant, because equity wealth sits with high-income, low-MPC households. Consumption kept rising after the dotcom bust.

theme_stances.key_argument: Post-GFC wealth gains came from stocks held by high-income, low-MPC households, so the consumption coefficient on wealth collapsed.
theme_stances.evidence: it is v much the consensus among investors
